name: Malaysia
summary: A federation formed in 1963 from independent Malaya (1957), Sabah, Sarawak and, until 1965, Singapore. It regards the history of Melaka and the Malay sultanates as its own, and grew into a multi-ethnic, newly industrialised economy.

location.value: Peninsular Malaysia and East Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo), separated by the South China Sea. It has 13 states and three federal territories.

terrain.value: Coastal plains, central mountain ranges and rainforest. Borneo has Mount Kinabalu (4,095 m) and great rivers such as the Rajang. Total area 330,803 km².

climate.value: Tropical and one of 17 “megadiverse” countries. Monsoon floods and seasonal haze (since the 1970s) are recurring problems.

resources.value: Historically tin and rubber, later oil and gas, palm oil and timber.
resources.source: Wikipedia: History of Malaysia (checked 5 Nov 2026); Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

disasters.value: Recurring floods (e.g. 1971, 2014–15, 2021–22), haze crises, the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, and the 2015 Sabah earthquake.

population.value: 32,447,385 in the 2020 census, and about 34.4 million estimated in 2026.

urbanisation.value: Rapid urbanisation from the 1980s. Kuala Lumpur is the capital and largest city; Putrajaya is the administrative centre.

disease.value: COVID-19 led to the Movement Control Order (2020–2021).

migration.value: Under British rule, Chinese and Indian immigration was encouraged for tin mining and rubber plantations, shaping today’s multi-ethnic society. In 2026, Bumiputera made up 70.6%, Chinese 22.1% and Indians 6.5%.

economicBase.value: Once reliant on agriculture and primary commodities (tin, rubber), now driven by services and manufacturing: a “newly industrialised economy”.

tradeRoutes.value: The Strait of Malacca shipping lane. Major trade with China, Singapore, the US and Japan. Electronics, palm oil and LNG exports.
tradeRoutes.source: Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

wealth.value: GDP per person about $15,981 (nominal) or $47,453 (PPP), 2026 estimates.

moneyAndTax.value: The ringgit (MYR). The 1997 Asian financial crisis “nearly caused the country’s currency, stock, and property markets to collapse, though they subsequently recovered.”

inequality.value: Gini 39.0 (2024, “medium inequality”). The New Economic Policy (1971) aimed to “eradicate poverty and restructure society to eliminate the identification of race with economic function”; Wikipedia describes it as controversial.

governmentType.value: A federal parliamentary constitutional elective monarchy. The King (Yang di-Pertuan Agong) is chosen from the nine state rulers every five years, and the Prime Minister leads the government.

keyRulers.value: Tunku Abdul Rahman (first prime minister). Tun Abdul Razak (launched the NEP, 1971). Mahathir Mohamad (1981–2003, 2018–2020). Najib Razak. Anwar Ibrahim (from 24 November 2022).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Malaysia (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: History of Malaysia (checked 5 Nov 2026)

succession.value: The King rotates among the state rulers. Prime ministers are chosen through parliamentary elections. The first change of ruling coalition since independence came in 2018, and the first hung parliament in 2022.

institutions.value: A Westminster-style parliament (Dewan Rakyat and Dewan Negara), a common-law legal system, and Islam as the official religion with freedom of religion for non-Muslims. The Rukun Negara national principles (1970).

stability.value: The 13 May 1969 race riots led to emergency rule, the suspension of parliament and the Rukun Negara. Later: the 1987 Operation Lalang arrests, constitutional crises, and political instability in 2020–2022.

eliteConflict.value: The 1MDB affair, “a major global corruption scandal” that implicated then-Prime Minister Najib Razak (2015), contributed to the 2018 change of government.

armyAndTech.value: Malaysian Armed Forces, with no conscription. Smaller than its neighbours’, and it relies partly on defence arrangements with Commonwealth partners.

majorWars.value: The Malayan Emergency (1948–1960), a communist insurgency against British and then Malayan rule. Konfrontasi with Indonesia (1963–1966). A second communist insurgency (1968–1989).

territoryChange.value: The Federation of Malaya (independent 31 August 1957) joined Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia (16 September 1963). Singapore separated in August 1965.

alliancesRivals.value: A founding member of ASEAN (1967). Territorial disputes include the South China Sea (Spratlys), Pedra Branca (with Singapore, decided 2008) and Ligitan and Sipadan (with Indonesia, decided 2002).

inventions.value: National projects: the Petronas Towers, the North–South Expressway, the Multimedia Super Corridor and the Proton national car.

scienceEducation.value: Mass public education in Malay, with Chinese and Tamil vernacular schools. Literacy rates are not stated in the sources checked.
scienceEducation.source: Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

openness.value: An open, trade-oriented economy that attracted foreign manufacturing investment from the 1970s onwards.

languageWriting.value: Malay (Bahasa Malaysia) is the official language, written in Latin script (Jawi is also used). English is “an active second language”. Chinese varieties, Tamil and indigenous languages are also spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Malay, Chinese, Indian and Bornean cultures, and Islamic and colonial architecture (Melaka, George Town UNESCO sites).
artsArchitecture.source: Andaya & Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed., 2017)

socialStructure.value: A multi-ethnic society. The Bumiputera policy grants the Malay majority and indigenous peoples a constitutionally recognised special position through affirmative-action measures, which is politically debated.

sharedIdentity.value: “Malaysia is a modern concept”. It regards the whole history of Malaya and Borneo, including Melaka, as its own. Motto: “Bersekutu Bertambah Mutu” (Unity is Strength).
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: History of Malaysia (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Malaysia (checked 5 Nov 2026)

neighbours.value: Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia, Brunei and the Philippines.

ideasReligions.value: A founding member of ASEAN, the OIC and the East Asia Summit, and a member of the Commonwealth and the Non-Aligned Movement.

colonisation.value: Colonised: Portuguese and Dutch Melaka, then British Malaya, Sarawak and North Borneo, and Japanese occupation (1941–45). Independent in 1957 (Malaya) and 1963 (Malaysia).

riseSignals.value: Negotiated independence (1957), defeat of the communist insurgency, commodity wealth, and export-led industrialisation from the 1970s–80s.

peakPeriod.value: Rapid growth in the late 1980s–1990s under Mahathir, before the 1997 crisis.

declineSignals.value: Not in decline. Current challenges named in the sources include political instability (2020–22), corruption (1MDB) and ethnic and religious tensions.

outcome.value: Ongoing: a federal constitutional monarchy and upper-middle-income economy (HDI 0.819, “very high”, 2023).

sources.value: Official statistics, census data and modern histories, checked against Wikipedia (“Malaysia” and “History of Malaysia”) on 5 Nov 2026. See also Andaya & Andaya (2017).

overallCertainty.value: High for dates and statistics. Interpretations of ethnic policy and recent politics are debated, so these entries quote neutral wording from the sources.
